title: A smaller Australia won’t be a stronger one
gist: The author, a former ambassador, argues that cutting immigration and international student numbers treats the symptom of underinvestment in housing, infrastructure and services, and would cost Australia skills, growth and regional influence; the answer is investment and productivity reform.

insights.claim: Australian political debate blames international students and migrants for pressure on housing, infrastructure, public services and cost of living, rather than years of poor policy choices and inadequate investment.
insights.speaker: Jenny Bloomfield
insights.so_what: Immigration-cut policies are being offered as a political fix; they may not address supply-side constraints.
insights.locator: Political debate and party policies now cast

insights.claim: Reducing immigration because investment has failed to keep pace treats the symptom, not the cause, and cutting international student numbers would weaken a major export industry and a source of talent, skills and influence.
insights.speaker: Jenny Bloomfield
insights.so_what: Lower intake would pressure education exports and labour supply; relevant for universities and sectors reliant on migrant labour.
insights.locator: Reducing immigration because investment has failed to keep pace

insights.claim: Migrants expand productive capacity, strengthen global networks and support a larger, more dynamic domestic market, but population growth must be sustainable and backed by investment in housing, infrastructure and services.
insights.speaker: Jenny Bloomfield
insights.so_what: Growth outcomes depend on infrastructure delivery matching population.
insights.locator: Immigration and an open, diverse society

insights.claim: The Colombo Plan brought about 40,000 young people from the region to study in Australia over three decades, and alumni became prime ministers, presidents, ministers and business leaders, making international education a diplomatic asset beyond an export industry.
insights.speaker: Jenny Bloomfield
insights.so_what: Student flows carry long-term soft-power value for Australia in Asia.
insights.locator: That insight helped inspire the Colombo Plan

insights.claim: When future leaders spend formative years in Australia they develop lasting affinity and instinctive understanding of its institutions, which is an extraordinary strategic asset Australia should seek more of.
insights.speaker: Jenny Bloomfield
insights.so_what: Cuts to student numbers carry a strategic cost not captured in near-term housing arguments.
insights.locator: When future leaders spend their formative years

insights.claim: Australia must lift productivity by creating rather than redistributing wealth, reducing unnecessary regulation, compliance costs and poorly targeted subsidies, improving workplace flexibility, and ensuring the immigration program delivers needed skills, while maintaining rigorous visa standards and expanding housing supply.
insights.speaker: Jenny Bloomfield
insights.so_what: Policy direction favours supply-side reform; progress on housing supply is a key indicator.

insights.claim: Australia's stable democracy, strong institutions, liveability and strategic position in the Indo-Pacific are real advantages, and a confident Australia should choose growth rather than turning inward.
insights.speaker: Jenny Bloomfield
insights.so_what: Frames the political choice between openness and restriction.
insights.quote: A confident Australia should choose growth.
insights.locator: In an uncertain and contested world
